a: The Great Wall of China is a series of fortifications built across the northern borders of China over approximately 2,000 years, from the 7th century BCE through the Ming Dynasty (1368–1644 CE). It was not constructed as a single continuous project but rather as successive walls built by different Chinese dynasties, each adding sections, repairing older ones, and extending the network. The primary purpose of the Great Wall was not merely to serve as an impassable barrier but as a comprehensive defensive system designed to protect Chinese states and empires from raids and invasions by nomadic groups from the Eurasian Steppe, particularly the Mongols and Xiongnu. The wall functioned as a military border control system featuring watchtowers, beacon towers for signaling, garrison stations, and troop barracks that allowed the military to monitor border movements, regulate trade along the Silk Road, and control immigration and emigration. The most famous and well-preserved sections date from the Ming Dynasty, when advanced construction techniques were employed. Builders used locally available materials: rammed earth in the west, stone blocks in mountainous regions, and kiln-fired bricks in the east. The wall incorporated natural barriers like rivers and mountain ridges. Construction relied on millions of laborers including soldiers, conscripted peasants, and convicts, and contrary to popular myth, human remains were not used as building materials. Official measurements from 2012 place the total length of all sections at 21,196 kilometers (13,171 miles), including 6,259 km of actual wall, 359 km of trenches, and 2,232 km of natural defensive barriers like hills and rivers. The wall's effectiveness is debated; it failed to prevent several major invasions, including the Mongol conquest under Genghis Khan in the 13th century. However, it did succeed in regulating trade, asserting sovereignty, and deterring smaller-scale raids. The wall was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987 and remains one of the world's most iconic historical structures, though only about 30% of the Ming wall sections remain in good condition today due to natural erosion and human damage.
